Intro (2 min)

Say: “These are all yours. Today we steal what worked and fix what cost marks.”

Start the lesson clock. The strip at the top shows planned timings, so you can see at a glance if you are behind.

Keys: Right arrow / Space next. Left arrow back. N notes. H hide bars. F fullscreen. T start slide timer.

Before you start: hand back the stories (activities 3 to 8 refer to them). No student devices are needed: the board is for everyone to look at, and you or a volunteer do the tapping. Every slide is tagged TALK (with a partner) or NOTEBOOK (write in the book).

Quotes were transcribed from handwriting. Check any you plan to dwell on.

1

Hall of Fame

Talk with your partner: which line is the best, and why? Hands up to vote.
Talk5 min
“Ima’s life was the same story again and again, wake up, school, sleep, wake up, school, sleep.”Repetition shows a boring routine0
“Maya’s smile disappeared like putting 100 kL of water on one small fire.”Simile: a surprising comparison0
“She felt as if a thousand feathers were tickling her guts.”Simile through the senses0
“Marie trembled as if she was having an inner earthquake.”Body shows fear0
“The house was full of emptiness and pure silence.”Silence builds dread0
“I wheezed, rasped and coughed, catching my breath so abruptly I thought I had drained all the oxygen out of this place.”Triple verb and hyperbole0
I think the best line is ___ because it makes me see / feel / hear ___.
Real lines from this class. Spelling tidied on praise lines.

Hall of Fame (5 min)

Do: TALK. 60 seconds in pairs to pick a winner. Count the hands and tap a card once per vote. Take 2 reasons, then reveal techniques.

Push: “Not ‘it’s good’. What exactly does the line DO to you?”

Bridge: “Next we steal three of these.”

Watch for: students praising length. Ask what the short line “Silence” does that a long one cannot.

2

Notebook: write the full sentence. Underline the technique you stole. Best line from each round is read aloud.

Steal Like a Writer (8 min)

Do: NOTEBOOK. Three rounds of 90 seconds, about 30 seconds sharing between. Tap New scene, then Go. Take 2 or 3 read-alouds per round.

Accept: any comparison that is specific and surprising. Reject “smelled bad” or “very scared”. Ask “bad like what?”

Watch for: fear described only with the word “scared”. Prompt: “What did his hands, knees or breath do?”

3

Splice Splitter

Notebook: copy each sentence with a splice and fix it. One is already correct.
Notebook8 min
Rule: a comma cannot join two sentences. Fix it with a full stop, and / but / so, or a semicolon.
0 / 6 splices fixed
Real sentences from this class. Check together: a volunteer taps the comma they changed.

Splice Splitter (8 min)

Do: NOTEBOOK. 3 minutes writing the corrected sentences, then a volunteer comes up and taps each wrong comma while the class checks their books. Sentence 4 is a trap: list commas are correct.

Accept for each fix: full stop, or a conjunction (and, but, so), or a semicolon. Sentence 6 needs two fixes.

Test: “Can each half stand alone as a sentence?” If yes, a comma is too weak.

Watch for: students over-correcting every comma. Sentence 5 is a strong line (“full of emptiness and pure silence”) spoiled by a splice: make the point that good writing needs clean punctuation.

4

Tense Trap

Talk with your partner: which six verbs slipped into the present tense?
Talk6 min
0 / 6 caught
Whisper first. Then a volunteer taps a verb and explains the fix. Spelling tidied so the tense errors stand out.

Tense Trap (6 min)

Do: TALK. 2 minutes whispering in pairs to spot all six, then a volunteer comes up and taps. Ask the class to say the correct past form aloud.

Intruders (6): is searching, finds, opens, hesitates, enters, smells. Past: was searching, found, opened, hesitated, entered, smelled.

Say: “Choose ONE tense for the whole story. For this task it is the past. Check every verb in your final read.”

Watch for: students “fixing” correct past verbs. Tapping those flashes a hint.

5

Speech Surgery

Notebook: copy each patient and fix it. 3 minutes. Then we operate together.
Notebook8 min
1. New speaker, new line.   2. Punctuation goes inside the speech marks.   3. Tag with a precise verb and an action.

Patient 1: punctuation

“Finish the job Sam”, whispered the man.
“Finish the job, Sam,” whispered the man.
Comma before a name. Comma inside the speech marks.

Patient 2: layout

“When did that get there?” he questioned “I must be dreaming,”.
“When did that get there?” he questioned. “I must be dreaming.”
Full stop after the tag. Speech ends inside the marks.

Patient 3: upgrade the tag

“Who… who are you… and… why do you… want me to go to the attic?” Tom mumbled, No response, just silence.
“Who… who are you?” Tom stammered, gripping his knife.
No response. Just silence.
Precise verb plus an action beat. Any strong version is fine.
Real lines from this class. Swap books with your partner and mark.

Speech Surgery (8 min)

Do: NOTEBOOK. 3 minutes copying and fixing all three. Tap Operate one at a time and the class compares with their own version. Partners swap books to mark.

Accept P1: “Finish the job, Sam,” whispered the man. P2: full stop after “questioned”, closing speech marks after the full stop. P3: any precise verb (stammered, whispered, gasped, croaked) plus an action beat.

Challenge: write a 4-line exchange between a hero and a mystery voice, with a different verb in every tag.

Watch for: “said” being replaced with random fancy verbs. Ask “would a person really growl that sentence?”

6

Show Me, Don’t Tell Me

Say it to your partner first. Then write your best version in your notebook.
Talk + notebook8 min
Each line: 20 seconds to say it aloud, 40 seconds to write it. Models are real, from this class.

Show Me, Don’t Tell Me (8 min)

Do: TALK then NOTEBOOK. Pick 3 or 4 of the 5, 60 seconds each: 20 seconds saying it to a partner, 40 seconds writing it. Take two attempts aloud before revealing the model.

Key teaching point (row 5): the writer already showed it (“legs shook, eyes flickered left and right”) then labelled it. Cut the label.

Prompt: body, senses, action. “What would a camera see?”

Watch for: showing lines that still contain the label (“he was scared and his hands shook”).

7

Cliffhanger Clinic

Talk: tense or flat? Then notebook: rewrite a FLAT ending.
Talk + notebook7 min
TENSE“Suddenly, the vines attacked!!!”Action stops the story at the peak. Needs more build-up and fewer exclamation marks.
TENSE“Then, a Beast appeared in front of him, that was the last thing he saw before darkness swallowed him.”Cuts off at the worst moment. The danger is shown.
FLAT“A new challenge has begun.”A label, not a moment. The writer tells us instead of putting us in it.
FLAT“The night arrived and he fell asleep with his gun next to him.”Sleeping releases the tension. Stop before the calm.
TENSE“She entered the Ogre of the Stones. She had made an easy choice: she strongly disliked toads.”A decision, a hook and a funny voice. Reader wants more.
TENSE“What is happening?” asked Evelyn. Hilda whispered, “They are here.”Short, unfinished threat. We do not see who “they” are.
Notebook, 90s: rewrite one FLAT ending.
Teacher taps once for TENSE, twice for FLAT as the class votes by hand.

Cliffhanger Clinic (7 min)

Do: TALK then NOTEBOOK. 2 minutes deciding in pairs, then a show of hands per card (you tap once for TENSE, twice for FLAT). Reveal, then 90 seconds writing a new ending in notebooks, then 2 read aloud.

Principle: end in the middle of the action, at the moment of danger or decision. Not on a label, a summary, or a sleep.

Toolkit to offer: a sound, a cut-off line, an unanswered question, a new threat.

Watch for: “Suddenly” on every ending. Ask for a sensory trigger instead (a crack, a smell, a shadow).

Check your first line. Does it grab the reader? Rewrite if not.

Today’s toolbox
SimileFear in the bodySmell comparisonTriple verbFull stop, not commaPast tense onlyNew speaker, new lineCliffhanger ending
Final check: tick these in your story

Exit ticket (8 min)

Timing: NOTEBOOK, then TALK. 5 minutes writing, 2 minutes pair share, 1 minute to collect.

Mark (ticket in books): 1 mark the weakest sentence correctly chosen, 1 mark a tool applied, 1 mark the result is clearly better.

Collect: look for who still writes comma splices and tense slips: those are the next-lesson groups.

Close: “Redraft next lesson with these fixes.”
